issues.legal_issue: Municipal authorities may require the current owner to address unauthorized building work even when that owner did not carry out the work.
material_facts: The respondent owned premises containing walls constructed without municipal sanction.
The respondent maintained that the walls were already present when she purchased the premises.
The municipality issued a notice requiring action concerning the unauthorized construction.
issues.conclusion: The municipality could take action against the respondent as the owner at the time of the notice, even if she had not constructed the walls.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 260(1)(a) and 478 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, must be read together and as a whole. Section 478 makes the owner at the time of notice liable where the person who carried out the unauthorized work is not then the owner. The building-regulation provisions should be construed to advance their purpose of protecting inhabitants’ safety, health, and well-being, while not extending statutory language to cases plainly outside its natural meaning.

predicates.municipal_enforcement_notice_challenge: A person challenged a municipal notice concerning building work.
predicates.unauthorized_work_without_permission: Building work was carried out without the required municipal permission.
predicates.current_owner_not_builder: The person who owned the premises when notice was given was not the person who carried out the work.

issues.definition: When a challenged municipal notice concerns work done without required permission and the current owner did not carry out that work, the current owner may be required to address it.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal notice is not invalid merely because it cites a different source of authority when the action is authorized under another applicable power.
material_facts: The municipality issued the challenged notice under a provision concerning unauthorized building work.
The notice was not issued under the separate provision that made the current owner liable for unauthorized work.
The statutory scheme authorized the municipality to require the current owner to address the unauthorized work.
issues.conclusion: The notice was not unauthorized or illegal merely because it was not issued under the provision relied on to support its validity.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory provision may be read with other provisions of the same enactment, and a lawful exercise of power may be supported by the power that authorizes it even if the notice cited a different provision. The Court relied on Pitamber Vajirshet v. Dhondu Navalapa, L. Hazari Mal Kuthiala v. Income-tax Officer, Special Circle, Ambala Cantt., Hukumchand Mills Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Nani Gopal Biswas v. The Municipality of Howrah. It also applied the principle that statutory language may receive an extended meaning when fairly susceptible of it to advance legislative purpose, but may not be strained to include cases plainly omitted from its natural meaning.

predicates.municipal_notice_validity_challenge: A person challenged the validity of a municipal notice.
predicates.notice_cites_different_power: The notice identified a source of authority different from the one supporting the challenged action.
predicates.alternative_lawful_authority_exists: The applicable legal framework empowered the municipality to take the challenged action under another source of authority.

issues.definition: If a challenged municipal notice cites a different power but another lawful authority supports the action, the notice is not invalid for that reference alone.
